metadata.title: Does the digital divide matter? Factors and conditions that promote ICT literacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2018 student microdata for two countries (Korea and Chile) and models a binary CIL achievement outcome derived from ICILS CIL scores. The manuscript states that data collection, coding, and reporting followed IEA quality standards, and it uses PV1 (PV1–PV5 are described) to represent each student’s CIL achievement score. However, the paper does not report whether ICILS sampling/survey weights or replicate weights were applied in the logistic regression analyses, nor does it name any weight variables. Because the analysis is a conventional logistic regression (not an ML algorithm that natively supports complex-survey weighting), the weighting approach is unclear; analysts should consult the ICILS Data User Guide for the appropriate student weight and replicate-weight variables if population-representative inference is required.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is constructed from ICILS CIL achievement using PV1 only, but the paper does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation) for either the PVs or the predictor variables. This is a reporting gap because ICILS datasets typically include missingness in background variables and PV-related components, and the choice of deletion vs. imputation can affect estimated odds ratios and model fit.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the ICILS 2018 Korea and Chile samples as selected countries with significant differences in CIL performance. The analytic sample is described as the participating students in each country (Korea: 2875; Chile: 3092). The paper does not report additional filtering beyond recoding predictor categories (gender, internet connection, computer experience, parents’ education) and dichotomizing CIL achievement using the ICILS standard cut-off at 500.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 (8th grade) Computer and Information Literacy (CIL), Korea
main_findings.target_variable: CIL achievement profile (successful vs low achieving; PV1; cut-off 500)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Overall model: Likelihood ratio χ²(4)=193.800, p<0.001; discrimination: c-statistic=69.4 (≈69% correct classification); goodness-of-fit: Hosmer–Lemeshow χ²(6)=5.826, p=0.443; pseudo R²: Cox & Snell=0.068, Nagelkerke=0.096. Significant predictors (Wald χ², p): COMPEX χ²(1)=83.766, p<0.001 (OR=2.189, 95% CI [1.851, 2.589]); S_INTNET χ²(1)=4.167, p=0.041 (OR=2.425, 95% CI [1.036, 5.677]); S_SEX χ²(1)=79.852, p<0.001 (OR=2.153, 95% CI [1.820, 2.547]); ISCED χ²(1)=19.359, p<0.001 (OR=1.491, 95% CI [1.248, 1.781]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 CIL data for Korea, the study leveraged Computer experience, Internet connection at home, Gender, and Parents’ level of education to predict CIL achievement profile (successful vs low achieving) using PV1, finding that all four predictors significantly increased the odds of being successful (largest odds ratio for computer experience). This indicates that strengthening students’ access to and sustained use of computers, alongside supporting home learning resources linked to parents’ education, may reduce the digital divide in ICT literacy, though the study’s use of PV1-only and unreported missing-data/weighting procedures limit precision and generalizability.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 (8th grade) Computer and Information Literacy (CIL), Chile
main_findings.target_variable: CIL achievement profile (successful vs low achieving; PV1; cut-off 500)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Overall model: Likelihood ratio χ²(4)=489.154, p<0.001; discrimination: c-statistic=68.9 (≈69% correct classification); goodness-of-fit: Hosmer–Lemeshow χ²(7)=5.735, p=0.571; pseudo R²: Cox & Snell=0.158, Nagelkerke=0.212. Significant predictors (Wald χ², p): COMPEX χ²(1)=90.602, p<0.001 (OR=2.173, 95% CI [1.852, 2.550]); S_INTNET χ²(1)=46.465, p<0.001 (OR=2.386, 95% CI [1.858, 3.063]); ISCED χ²(1)=211.097, p<0.001 (OR=3.488, 95% CI [2.947, 4.129]); S_SEX χ²(1)=14.491, p<0.001 (OR=1.357, 95% CI [1.160, 1.589]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 CIL data for Chile, the study leveraged Computer experience, Internet connection at home, Gender, and Parents’ level of education to predict CIL achievement profile (successful vs low achieving) using PV1, finding that all four predictors significantly increased the odds of being successful, with parents’ education showing the strongest association. This indicates that policies targeting family-level educational resources and home connectivity—together with opportunities for sustained computer experience—may be especially important for improving ICT literacy outcomes, while the reliance on PV1-only and unreported missing-data/weighting procedures constrain causal interpretation and population inference.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) in two countries (Korea: n=2875; Chile: n=3092) and models a binary CIL achievement outcome using the ICILS standard cut-off at 500 (successful vs low achieving). Although ICILS provides five plausible values (PV1–PV5), the authors conduct the analyses using PV1 only. For Korea, the logistic model is significant (likelihood ratio χ²(4)=193.800, p<0.001) with c-statistic=69.4 and Hosmer–Lemeshow χ²(6)=5.826 (p=0.443); all predictors (computer experience, home internet, gender, parents’ education) are significant, with computer experience showing the largest odds ratio (OR=2.189). For Chile, the model is also significant (χ²(4)=489.154, p<0.001) with c-statistic=68.9 and Hosmer–Lemeshow χ²(7)=5.735 (p=0.571); parents’ education has the strongest association (OR=3.488). Limitations include unreported missing-data handling and unclear use of ICILS sampling/replicate weights, and the use of PV1-only may understate uncertainty compared with proper PV combining.
